In a new interview, Knightley opened up about fans approaching her and quoting the film, but it doesn’t mean much to her. “I have not watched Love Actually since the premiere, which was when I was 18,” Knightley said in an interview with Heart . “So, I think I’m the person that knows it the least of anybody.” She continued, “I know that people have a particular look on their face and then they say things to me and I know that means they’re quoting Love Actually, but I don’t really know what it is. The scene is one of the most remembered, but for Knightley, it was only a week of filming when she was 17 and didn’t leave a lasting impact. title: ‘Here There Are Blueberries’ Broadway Review: Evil As Banal As A Bowl Of Fruit
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Here There Are Blueberries’ Broadway Review: Evil As Banal As A Bowl Of Fruit ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Historical Musical Plays With Gospel Truth Richard Lloyd Dies: Guitarist With Influential Punk Pioneers Television Was 75 View All November 9, 2026 7:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michelle Beck, Delia Cunningham, Kathleen Chalfant, 'Here There Are Blueberries' Matthew Murphy Here There Are Blueberries , the exceptional Pulitzer finalist docu-drama that opened Off Broadway two years ago to great admiration, finally makes its Broadway debut tonight at the Barrymore Theatre. The play, about a mysterious real-life cache of one-of-a-kind Auschwitz photos submitted to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in 2007, remains as intriguing as ever – and with source material as grotesquely mesmerizing as these candid snapshots, how could it not? In fact, the sheer emotional heft of that photo album and everything it suggests dominates Blueberries to an extent that the play itself can seem rather thin at times, not entirely unworthy of the material at hand but not on equal footing either. Revelations about the banality of evil carry a force no matter how familiar we are with the concept, but familiar we are, and Blueberries can feel somewhat naive at times in its presumption that no one in the audience has ever heard of Hannah Arendt. But in the grand scheme of things, and in light of the historical tale being told here, those quibbles with dramaturgy shouldn’t diminish the real achievement that is Here There Are Blueberries . The play is vital and more often than not riveting. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News ‘Other Desert Cities’ Review: Julia Louis-Dreyfus Gets Seriously Funny For Broadway Debut News ‘860’ Broadway Review: Billy Crystal Remembers The Stuff Of Life And Loss Performed by an excellent cast – any production that features the great Kathleen Chalfant is an opportunity not to be missed – Here There Are Blueberries is, at its core, a detective tale. In 2007, a young Holocaust museum archivist named Rebecca Erbelding (Delia Cunningham) receives a letter at her D.C. office from a man who wants to donate a cache of WWII snapshots. Delia Cunningham, Kathleen Chalfant, Michael Cerveris Matthew Murphy The offer isn’t unusual – the museum serves as a repository for such keepsakes – but the nature of his collection most certainly is. The photo collection long in the man’s possession is more than a rarity, it’s absolutely unique: The images are of Nazi officers – including some of the highest ranking and most notorious, from Mengele to Höss – in their living quarters just over the wall from the camp’s atrocities. Some are of an almost surreal vacation lodge a few miles away, where officers, SS guards and female office workers alike would be treated to days of rest and relaxation for jobs well done. One officer is given five days there for his murder of two Jews attempting to escape the camp. Such images had never been observed in photographs before, and their discovery is nothing less than historic, generating headlines across the globe, with much of the public fascination falling on the young German female camp office workers enjoying their vacation lodge days and food-and-drink treats. “Here,” says the caption (in German) of one such photo, “there are blueberries.” The play is structured as an investigation, lead by the young archivist, as the museum staff seeks to uncover the circumstances under which these snapshots were taken, who took them, who is pictured, and, perhaps most intriguingly, how on earth did they survive when all over such evidence was destroyed by the Nazis themselves as the regime fell? One such question – how did the man who possesses the photos discover them? – is easily answered: A retired U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel (Michael Cerveris) found the album in the abandoned apartment he briefly inhabited while stationed in Frankfort at the end of the war. Why he kept them in his possession, and did so secretly, is unknowable – he died shortly after making the museum donation. Other questions posed by the photos are of a more philosophical nature. Did those seemingly carefree young women at the lodge have any idea that the office work they were doing contributed to the genocide next door? And if so, how could they ? Conrad Ricamora (foreground, right) Matthew Murphy Blueberries , for all its demands on facing harsh truths, plays a bit coy in feigning shock at the answers, as if Judgment At Nuremberg never existed, an excusable but still noticeable manipulation. A bit more difficult to overlook are other red herrings seemingly designed to give the play momentum, such as will the museum board accept the donation of the Nazi photos when its mission is to chronicle the victims, not the victimizers? It’s a stick man argument. Blueberries is on sturdier dramatic ground when new characters – the relatives of the Nazis and camp workers in the photographs – begin arriving mid-show to offer their perspectives. The sister of an office worker sticks with the usual denials, but others are revelatory, not least the grandson of Rudolph Höss, who relates an unnerving tale of his family’s complicity and his own struggles with the violence he fears is an inheritance. The grandson’s tale is riveting, as is Brandon Flynn’s performance, a stand-out in a uniformly excellent cast that, in addition to those mention above, includes Conrad Ricamora, Scott Barrow, Michelle Beck and Montego Glover, all playing a variety of roles. Derek McLane’s stark set design, dominated by the many tall-legged stand-up desks used by the museum archivists to study the photos, is stellar, as are the crucial projections (designed by David Bengali) that allows us to see what the archivists are seeing. The photos projected onto the walls would be transfixing even without the superb lighting design (David Lander) and sound design (Bobby McElver) that further an entirely earned mood of dread and even despair, never more so than during a late scene that finally gives all those unseen victims their moment in this story, and in a manner so wrenching it won’t be spoiled here except to say that another photo album enters the story, and its story of survival is every bit as astonishing as the first. Brandon Flynn Matthew Murphy In the end, Here There Are Blueberries has sailed past its own here-and-there shortcomings to land on a final thought, artfully told and with clarity of conviction: Just imagine how many untold boxes of forgotten family memorabilia and grim relics are waiting to be discovered, with secrets as efficiently hidden as those sealed away in the human heart? title: Steve Buscemi Reveals Which Show He Refuses to Appear on: “I Don’t Care How Much You Paid Me”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All November 9, 2026 6:39pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Steve Buscemi Theo Wargo/Getty Images If you were hoping to see Steve Buscemi take on the hot wings challenge, don’t bet on it. During a recent appearance on the Happy Sad Confused podcast , host Josh Horowitz asked the veteran actor, who’s promoting his new films Wild Horse Nine and Klara and the Sun , about things he dislikes. “I’m confused why people like spicy food, why they like their mouths hot,” Buscemi replied. So First We Feast’s Hot Ones , hosted by Sean Evans , likely won’t ever be a stop on the actor’s press tours. Related Stories Movies 'Klara and the Sun' Review: Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams Should Have Insisted on a Factory Reset for Taika Waititi's Cloying, Clumsy AI Fable Movies John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell Buddy Up for London Film Festival Premiere of 'Wild Horse Nine' “Sam Rockwell told me that he and Parker Posey did Hot Ones — that’s something I would never do. I don’t care how much you paid me, how much they said, ‘But it would really support the film,’ no. It not only makes me confused, it makes me angry,” he added with a laugh. “You’ll never get me, Hot Ones !” In recent years, Hot Ones , which launched in 2015, has become a routine stop for celebrities as they’re making the rounds to promote their latest projects. The YouTube talk show, created by Evans and Christopher Schonberger, sees the host interviewing guests as they eat a platter of ten wings, each coated in a progressively hotter hot sauce. Dozens of celebrities have taken on the challenge, including Jennifer Lawrence, Paul Rudd, Billie Eilish, Post Malone, Conan O’Brien, Charlize Theron, Pedro Pascal and Shaquille O’Neal, among others. But seeing many stars end in tears or yell in pain (“I feel like I’m gonna die,” Lawrence said during her episode) likely wasn’t a selling point for Buscemi. Earlier this year, Evans revealed some of his favorite Hot Ones episodes during a chat with Matt Belloni. “I always say if you’re new to the show, check out the Conan O’Brien episode or the Gordon Ramsay episode. Jennifer Lawrence is another one or Maya Rudolph. Paul Rudd is a classic. Charlize Theron,” he said at the time. “I always say to start with those. If you like those episodes, you’ll probably like the show. If you don’t like those episodes, stop there. There’s nothing for you.” THR

title: LISTEN: ‘Roland Martin Unfiltered’ Rides Midterm Elections Momentum After Historic Vote
full_text: × Nov 9, 2026 6:37pm PT LISTEN: ‘Roland Martin Unfiltered’ Rides Midterm Elections Momentum After Historic Vote Variety's 'Strictly Business' podcast features conversations with industry leaders about the business of media and entertainment By Cynthia Littleton Plus Icon Cynthia Littleton Business Editor @Variety_Cynthia Latest LISTEN: ‘Roland Martin Unfiltered’ Rides Midterm Elections Momentum After Historic Vote 2 hours ago WME Streamlines Motion Picture Lit and Talent Departments, Promotes Will Ward to Lead Fashion 11 hours ago Mike Lee and Darren Yan Unveil ISO, a Next-Generation Management Firm Specializing in Creators, Live Streamers, Gaming and Music 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source On today’s episode of Variety ‘s “Strictly Business” podcast, digital news entrepreneur Roland Martin discusses the growth of his “ Roland Martin Unfiltered ” program and how it gained momentum during the buildup to this last week’s historic midterm elections. Martin’s daily political news and commentary roundtable program went on a barnstorming tour over the three weeks leading up to Election Day on Nov. 3. The show targeted key areas in the South and Southeast where the protection of voting rights, affordability, the relentless GOP attack on DEI and other issues had already fired up voters. Related Stories Netflix Orders YA Drama 'Prep' Based on Curtis Sittenfeld Novel From Nicole Taylor 'Love Is Blind' Star Rob Feeley Breaks His Silence on Michaella, the Beekeeper and Why He Nearly Skipped the Reunion “Twelve cities in fifteen days. It was Little Rock, Arkansas. Fairfax, Virginia. Lansing, Michigan. We came home for a day. Then it was like Indianapolis, Atlanta and then we were in Jackson, Mississippi, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, Miami Gardens, West Palm Beach, Tallahassee, Florida. Back to Atlanta and Lithonia, Georgia again. Baton Rouge. then. Arlington, Texas. Dallas, Texas. Houston, Texas. Fort Bend County. And then came home two days before the election,” Martin says. “It was absolutely crazy. the first week I had our 35-foot bus on the road. And then that second week I had that and the Sprinter [van] on the road. And we were flying into a city, doing the show, go to the hotel, put all of our suitcases in the Sprinter and then would just pack overnight clothes. They would drive to the next city overnight. We would then fly to the next city. Uber to the hotel, check in. Go set up. Do the show. Repeat, rinse, repeat. I was a show host, a producer, a travel agent, a logistical coordinator. It was crazy.” Martin, an alumnus of CNN, TV One and Tom Joyner’s radio program, says the tour reflected the freedom and flexibility offered by working in digital media. And it all has the potential to reach viewers in a different way than a traditional news program. “What’s so different from linear is that you’re really touching viewers. You’re really communicating with them. I’m not spending three, four, five, six minutes on a segment. Sometimes I’m doing twenty, thirty minutes doing deep dives,” Martin says. “I’m not trying to do a mainstream show. I am not trying to replicate MS NOW, CNN, ABC, NBC, CBS, Fox News, or any of those people. We break all the rules. We’re not trying to be slick. I’ll grab my DJI action camera and I’m shooting stuff and it’s totally unconventional. title: ‘Summer School, 2001,’ the First Czech-Vietnamese Feature, Is Coming to America via Cinemas, Amazon (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 9, 2026 6:31pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Summer School, 2001' Courtesy of KVIFF In 2025, Summer School, 2001 , the debut feature of writer-director Dužan Duong and dubbed the “first Czech-Vietnamese feature film,” made a splash at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival and beyond. Now, it is coming to America, courtesy of Reel Citrus, an L.A.-based distributor of Asian and diaspora films. The company will open Summer School, 2001 in a limited U.S. theatrical release on Dec. 11 at Cinemark cinemas, hitting screens before Dune 3 and Avengers: Doomsday opens a week later. The film will then stream on Amazon from Dec. 18 before rolling out globally. Related Stories Movies Claes Bang, Valerie Pachner Drama 'I Is Another' Sells Wide Ahead of AFM Business The Hollywood Reporter Launches Turkish Edition “At a time when immigration and belonging are front-page news in both the U.S. and Europe, the release brings two diasporas into the same theater,” said Reel Citrus. Summer School, 2001 follows 17-year-old Kien, who returns to his family’s market stall in Cheb, a small town on the Czech border, after spending 10 years in Vietnam. It becomes a chaotic summer, during which the family must try to become whole again. After its Karlovy Vary world premiere, the movie drew more than 20,000 moviegoers during its run in Czech cinemas. At the Czech Lion Awards, the Czech national film honors, Summer School, 2001 won the best screenplay award for Duong, Jan Smutný and Lukáš Kokeš, along with the best supporting actor honor for Dũng Nguyễn, the first Vietnamese actor to win a Czech Lion. The Czech Film Critics’ Awards named it the best screenplay and the Discovery of the Year. ‘Summer School, 2001’ Courtesy of KVIFF At Viet Film Fest, the largest U.S. festival for the Vietnamese diaspora, the film won the Bronze Drum (Trống Đồng) Award for the best feature film, the best actor honor for Tô Tiến Tài and the Audience Choice Award for best feature. Reel Citrus says it chose the theaters to target the communities that the film, which is in Vietnamese and Czech with English subtitles, speaks to. Most of the cinemas are in areas with large Vietnamese American populations, including Southern California, where it plays in Huntington Beach next to Little Saigon, the Bay Area, Houston, Dallas, Seattle, Las Vegas and the Washington, D.C. area. The rest of the theaters are in Chicago, Cleveland, Pittsburgh and Central Texas, “home to strong Czech, Polish and other Central and Eastern European communities,” the company explains. Vietnamese American families and Czech and Polish moviegoers came out in droves for a screening of Summer School, 2001 at the Avalon Theatre in Washington, D.C. last March. Co-presented with the Embassy of the Czech Republic, it served as an early test for Reel Citrus, which says it releases films “in person, one community at a time.” Reel Citrus acquired North American rights across all media, along with worldwide streaming rights, to Summer School, 2001 from AZN kru. “ Summer School, 2001 was an eye-opening film for us,” said Brittany Tran, founder & managing director of Reel Citrus. “Many of us grew up knowing the Vietnamese American story, but we knew far less about the Vietnamese families who built their lives in the Czech Republic and across Europe. Our diaspora is global, and when Vietnamese communities in the U.S. see the communities in Europe, we realize how much we share.” Dužan Duong, courtesy of Karlovy Vary International Film Festival She added: “We know we’re opening the week before Dune and Avengers , so we’re competing with the gods. But audiences who rarely see their own stories on the big screen are exactly who this release is for.” And Duong, who talked to THR about his creative vision for Summer School, 2001 and his other creative work, shared: “Vietnamese families have been part of Czech life for decades, but our stories rarely reach the screen. I made this film for my community in Cheb and for every family that has had to find its way back to each other. Seeing it open in American theaters, in front of Vietnamese and Czech audiences together, means more than I can say.” Check out a trailer for Summer School, 2001 here. THR

title: How the American French Film Festival Is Bringing French Cinema to 3,000 Los Angeles High School Students With Packed Screenings of ‘In Waves’
full_text: × Nov 9, 2026 6:11pm PT How the American French Film Festival Is Bringing French Cinema to 3,000 Los Angeles High School Students With Packed Screenings of ‘In Waves’ By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest How the American French Film Festival Is Bringing French Cinema to 3,000 Los Angeles High School Students With Packed Screenings of ‘In Waves’ 2 hours ago French Judo Legend Teddy Riner Announces 2027 Presidential Bid, Drawing Praise From Emmanuel Macron 3 hours ago Prime Video, Scanbox Entertainment Team on New ‘Hamilton’ Films and TV Series Based on Bestselling Swedish Spy Franchise (EXCLUSIVE) 8 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Philip Guerette The American French Film Festival , which celebrated its 30th anniversary this year, has been on a journey to cultivate a new generation of French movie lovers for two decades with its educational program for Los Angeles high school students. This milestone edition brought around 3,000 students to the DGA theater for five packed screenings of “In Waves,” Phuong Mai Nguyen’s heart-wrenching animated feature which was bought Netflix at Cannes. Related Stories 'KPop Demon Hunters,' 'Squid Game' Stars Fete Netflix's Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases 'Tantara,' 'All of Us Are Dead' Season 2 'Stranger Things' Prequel Spinoff 'Other Worlds' Ordered to Series at Netflix Adapted from AJ Dungo’s graphic novel at set in Southern California, “In Waves” is a love story between a shy teenage boy and the girl who teaches him how to surf and how to live, before she succumbs to cancer. The screenings, which drew applause and tears throughout, also gave students the opportunity to engage in the post-screening Q&A with the film’s producer, Priscilla Bertin , and screenwriter Fanny Burdino. Philip Guerette Spearheaded by Anouchka Van Riel , the festival deputy director, the program brings together more than 60 schools over five days, with roughly half coming from the public school system and half from private institutions. It also reaches beyond French-language classes to students studying performing arts and other creative disciplines. In an interview with Variety , Van Riel discussed the importance of the programme to allow younger audiences to discover international cinema at a time when arthouse moviegoers are aging and foreign-language films face growing challenges in U.S. theaters. She also talked about the program’s rapid growth, why subtitles are no longer the barrier they once were, and the powerful response to “In Waves” which Netflix is positioning in the Awards race. How many students and schools participate in the program? We have more than 60 schools participating over five days, so that’s more than 12 schools a day. We organize five screenings of the same film, each with around 600 students. That’s approximately 3,000 students every year. I’ve built a database of around 300 schools, and we start reaching out in May. Within a week of sending the first email, half the seats — around 1,500 — are already booked. Then I spend the summer filling the remaining places. There’s enormous demand. We also make a point of having a mix of public and private schools, roughly 50/50. That’s very important to us. For public schools, transportation can be a challenge. Some have to apply for grants just to pay for the buses. There’s an entire economy around organizing these trips, and a lot depends on the teachers. Philip Guerette How does the festival work with teachers to prepare students for the screenings? We work with the American Association of Teachers of French, which prepares two educational guides, one in French and one in English. The French-language guide is around 100 pages long. It’s incredibly detailed and allows teachers to explore the film from multiple perspectives, including its themes and cinematic language. The guides are designed to help students study the film before or after the screening. And we don’t just work with French-language classes. Around half of the participating classes are English-speaking. Many Los Angeles high schools have performing arts programs, and those students come because they’re interested in cinema and want to meet the filmmakers. The majority of these kids have never attended a film screening followed by a Q&A. That’s something we want to change. That’s surprising in Los Angeles, where the film industry is everywhere. It’s extraordinary. I’m a member of the Producers Guild, and I receive invitations to screenings and conversations with filmmakers almost every day. There are incredible events happening constantly, but these kids don’t have access to them. Of course, if their parents work in the industry, that’s different. But otherwise, most students aren’t exposed to that world. I grew up in a small town in Alsace, and I remember my French teacher taking us to the movies all the time when I was in middle school. Some of those screenings even had Q&As. There’s a tradition of that in France that doesn’t really exist here in the same way. We used to organize masterclasses for university students, including at USC, but we realized it was difficult to attract them. They’re already surrounded by so many opportunities on campus. With high school students, we can work directly through the teachers. That’s how we’ve developed this program. Is the goal ultimately to cultivate a younger audience for French cinema? Absolutely. It’s about renewing the audience. A couple of years ago, we screened “The Marching Band,” and when the film was eventually released theatrically in the U.S., I was invited to moderate a Q&A. I loved the film, so I was very happy to do it. But the theater was only half full, and I don’t think there was a single person under 65. That’s the problem. Foreign-language films have traditionally been considered niche in the U.S. Streaming platforms have helped change that perception somewhat, but we still need to familiarize younger audiences with these films. That’s why this program is so important. Are subtitles still an obstacle for younger American audiences? Not nearly as much as people think. We’ve conducted surveys with students after the screenings, and more than 80% say subtitles aren’t a barrier to watching foreign-language films. It’s not a completely scientific study, but it gives us a good indication of how attitudes are changing. Between streaming platforms, social media and series like “Squid Game,” young people have become accustomed to watching subtitled content. Sometimes there’s still a little hesitation before the screening. But once they’re sitting in the theater, they realize it’s easy. I really don’t think subtitles are the problem for this generation anymore. Distribution is a major part of the problem. That’s why streaming platforms have become so important for the circulation of foreign-language films. But there’s also the question of exposure. If young people aren’t given opportunities to discover these films, they’re not necessarily going to seek them out themselves. In Waves Courtesy of Netflix This year’s selection was “In Waves.” What made it particularly suitable for the program? There’s a wonderful connection between this film and the festival. The producer, Priscilla Bertin, had already come to the festival two years ago with “Wild Diamond,” and at the time she was in post-production on “In Waves.” We became familiar with the project very early, and it made complete sense for us to bring it back this year. What’s interesting is that the film is based on an American graphic novel that was discovered by a French producer in a secondhand bookstore in France and developed into a movie. We explain that background to the students before the screenings, including why it’s considered a French film and the response has been extraordinary. The screenings were packed, and the students seemed particularly moved by the film. What was the atmosphere like? It was very striking. At the first screening, I went straight into introducing the filmmakers for the Q&A, and I realized something wasn’t right because the students were still processing what they’d just watched. Usually, when a film ends, the students immediately line up to ask questions. But with “In Waves,” it took time. Every day, there was this moment of silence. The film had affected them so deeply that they needed a little time before they could speak. There’s something cathartic about sitting in a dark theater with other people, crying together and sharing the same emotions. You feel safe because everyone is experiencing that grief together. I think young people have fewer opportunities to experience cinema that way now. That’s what made these screenings so special. title: French Judo Legend Teddy Riner Announces 2027 Presidential Bid, Drawing Praise From Emmanuel Macron
full_text: × Nov 9, 2026 5:28pm PT French Judo Legend Teddy Riner Announces 2027 Presidential Bid, Drawing Praise From Emmanuel Macron By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest How the American French Film Festival Is Bringing French Cinema to 3,000 Los Angeles High School Students With Packed Screenings of ‘In Waves’ 3 hours ago French Judo Legend Teddy Riner Announces 2027 Presidential Bid, Drawing Praise From Emmanuel Macron 3 hours ago Prime Video, Scanbox Entertainment Team on New ‘Hamilton’ Films and TV Series Based on Bestselling Swedish Spy Franchise (EXCLUSIVE) 8 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Credit: Banijay French judo superstar Teddy Riner , a five-time Olympic gold medalist and multiple world champion, has announced that he is running for president of France in 2027 in a fiery speech posted on social media. The athlete, who has never held political office but is one of France’s most recognizable and popular sporting figures, portrayed himself as a political outsider determined to stand for ordinary French citizens which he feels have been let down. Related Stories Netflix Stock Deflates to Two-Year Low. What Will It Take to Revive Revenue Growth? Netflix Names Mattel Executive Roberto Stanichi as VP of Consumer Products and Experiences Riner’s announcement comes at a particularly turbulent moment in France, just five months before a presidential election that has exposed deep divisions across the political spectrum. The far-right party Rassemblement National is dominating the polls by a wide margin, with Marine Le Pen drawing between 33% and 37% of first-round voting intentions in recent surveys, roughly twice the support of her closest rivals. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who leads the radical-left party La France Insoumise, has been gaining ground and is polling at around 17% to 19%, while the political center remains fragmented, with no candidate emerging to succeed Emmanuel Macron . The country has also been rocked by weeks of mass protests over the soaring cost of living and conditions in schools which escalated into violent riots. “My name is Teddy Riner, and today I’m telling you straight to your face: I am a candidate in the 2027 presidential election,” he said while facing the camera and sitting at a desk in a presidential-style setting while bookshelves and a tricolor French flag in the background. La résignation n'est pas une option. Face aux difficultés de notre pays, l'heure est venue de prendre ses responsabilités.⁰⁰Je suis candidat à l'élection présidentielle de 2027. ⁰⁰ #TeddyRiner2027 #Présidentielle2027 #LaFrancequonveut pic.twitter.com/nM7rTfyTrH — Teddy Riner (@teddyriner) November 9, 2026 “I know what people are going to say about me: ‘He’s crazy,’ ‘He’s not part of the establishment,’ ‘He doesn’t know the rules,’ ‘He’s never been involved in politics.’ But ask yourselves this question: What is really crazy today?” Riner went on to paint a bleak picture of France, citing growing public debt, economic hardship and a breakdown of law and order. “Is it crazy to refuse to watch France collapse under the weight of its debt, a little more every day? To see a country so rich pretend that it is poor?” he asked. Riner criticized what he described as an unfair system that places an excessive burden on working people. “Is it crazy to reject the hypocrisy of a system where those who get up early, work hard and follow the rules have no choice but to pay for everyone else?” Macron reacted warmly to Riner’s announcement in an interview with the French broadcaster France 5 welcoming his decision to enter politics and praising his sense of duty. “Teddy Riner is a tremendous athlete who makes our country proud,” Macron said. “I supported him in competitions and as an athlete, and he is a committed man.” Macron, who cannot seek a third consecutive presidential term in 2027, applauded the prospect of citizens from outside the political establishment taking part in the national debate. “Political life, the life of the nation, does not belong to professionals,” Macron said, alluding to his own path, as he came into politics a decade ago after working in investment banking at Rothschild. “The life of the nation belongs to women and men who want to give their time, who are ready to commit themselves and fight difficult battles to make our country better. I am very happy that someone like Teddy Riner, who is a great champion, has decided to take part in this presidential debate and bring his convictions, his ideas and his talent,“ Macron continued. title: Johnny Depp & Ti West Land In A Chilly London For ‘Ebenezer’ Global Premiere
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Johnny Depp & Ti West Land In A Chilly London For ‘Ebenezer’ Global Premiere Diane Warren Talks Emotion At Working With Andrea Bocelli On ‘Maserati: The Brothers’ Song: “I Was Sobbing” – Sound & Screen Film Japanese Horror Manga ‘Noah Of The Blood Sea’ Set For Feature Adaptation As Tyrus Pictures Options Rights View All November 9, 2026 5:24pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Johnny Depp attends the "Ebenezer" Global Premiere at Odeon Luxe Leicester Square Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures Christmas came early to London’s Leicester Square on Monday as Johnny Depp touched down for a red-carpet global premiere of Ebenezer in the company of director Ti West and cast including Rupert Grint, Sam Claflin, Tramell Tillman, Ellie Bamber and Robert Strong. The red carpet was decked out with Christmas trees and artificial snow while 1950s festive classics blasted out in the backdrop, and if by magic, temperatures dropped, ending an unseasonably balmy autumn. The chilly conditions did not deter fans who crammed into the red-carpet enclosure, most of them there for a glimpse of Depp. He did not disappoint, arriving in a timely fashion to talk to handpicked media and then walk the fan line. Related Stories News Johnny Depp Open To Reprising 'Pirates Of The Caribbean' Role To "Send Them Off On A Better Note" Documentary Joe Perry Bows Out Of Hollywood Vampires Doc Screening As Aerosmith Ramps Up For Hollywood Bowl Gigs Johnny Depp attends the “Ebenezer” Global Premiere at Odeon Luxe Leicester Square Photo by Tristan Fewings/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures Depp’s latest role as Ebenezer Scrooge is being billed as the actor’s comeback, after being left out in cold following his high-profile legal battles with ex-wife Amber Heard. Watch on Deadline Rumors are rife that if Ebenezer performs well, it could help green-light a reboot of the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise with Depp reprising his Captain Jack Sparrow role. Whether this comes to pass remains to be seen but it was plain to see on Monday night that Depp was the main draw, with the public at least appearing to have moved on. Talking to Deadline on the red carpet, West said he and Depp had bonded over a shared love of Charles Dickens’ ‘A Christmas Carol’ as well as admiration for Alastair Sim’s performance as Ebenezer Scrooge in an 1951 adaptation. ´Ebenezer’ director Ti West talks on casting Johnny Depp as Ebenezer Scrooge: “He [Depp] was obsessed with Scrooge since he was a little kid. When he found out about the movie, he was like, ‘Alistair Sims is a huge reason why I’m even an actor.’” pic.twitter.com/A2zFDV8J5r — Deadline (@DEADLINE) November 9, 2026 “I’ve been obsessed with it since I was little kid. I would read it every Christmas, and I was into it because it was a ghost story and then I saw the George C. Scott film when I was really little and Marley really scared me,” he said referring to Clive Donner’s 1984 version. “I’ve had a fascination of it and a version in my head that I was waiting for someone to make that they didn’t make. What’s also cool about it is that it’s one of the rare stories that because it’s so enduring, redoing it, is part of the charm,” he said. West said Depp had approached him about the role when he heard the production was in the works. “He was obsessed with Scrooge since when he was a little kid also which I didn’t know and so when he found about the movie he was like, ‘Alastair Sim is a huge reason why I am even an actor.’ It was a weird cosmic thing where it was meant to be,” said West. Depp confirmed West’s account in a public interview ahead of heading inside the cinema. “I adored it as a child and to this day I know there is no better person to play Ebenezer Scrooge than Alastair Sim… the challenge is to find another angle,” said Depp, praising West for creating a atmosphere on set in which there was space to experiment with the role. title: Ariana Grande on First Time Meeting Ben Stiller: “Directing Me in an Orgy Scene in ‘Zoolander 2’”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All November 9, 2026 4:59pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Ariana Grande and Jimmy Fallon on 'The Tonight Show.' Todd Owyoung/NBC Ariana Grande won’t be forgetting the first time she met Ben Stiller anytime soon. During a recent episode of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon , Grande, Stiller and Robert De Niro made a joint appearance to chat about their new film Focker-in-Law , which releases on Nov. 25. At one point, host Jimmy Fallon asked the Grammy-winning singer about the first time she met Stiller, to which she replied, “I met Ben in a very different way,” drawing laughter from the audience. Related Stories TV Alex Warren to Host Kids' Choice Awards, Airing on CBS for the First Time; Taylor Swift Leads Nominees General News Pete Davidson Slams Body Shaming of Ex-Fiancée Ariana Grande “He was directing me in an orgy scene in Zoolander 2 with a hippo and Susan Sarandon,” she revealed. In the 2016 action-comedy, directed by Stiller, Derek (Stiller) and Hansel (Owen Wilson) are lured into the fashion world again, in Rome, where they find themselves the target of a sinister conspiracy. Grande makes a cameo as part of Hansel’s eccentric romantic circle, which he calls his “orgy” group. “So right off the bat, we had a comfortability,” Grande added, as Stiller quipped that they had an instant connection due to the unusual encounter. “It sounds like two truths and a lie, but it’s my reality,” the Wicked star said. The pair have now reunited in Focker-in-Law , which sees Greg (Stiller) and Pam Focker’s (Teri Polo) son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) get wrapped up in family chaos when he decides to marry a strong-willed woman, Olivia Jones (Grande), who appears to be his complete mismatch. The “Petal” singer also told Fallon that their first scene together in Focker-in-Law was another interesting experience. “We were thrust into rehearsing the Heimlich scene, where I give you [Stiller] the Heimlich,” Grande said. “So I thought maybe we’ll sit in [director] John [Hamburg’s] office with a script and talk a little, get to know each other a little more and work on the scenes and talk about Greg and Olivia.” “But no. We met the stunts team, and they were amazing. And they were like, ‘All right, Ben, bend over. Ariana, you’ll get behind and just put your arms around him.’ And I was like, ‘Oh, perfect. Yeah,'” she added with a laugh. “My mom was like, ‘How was your first day, honey?’ I was like, ‘Well, I gave Ben Stiller the Heimlich for a few hours.’ It was crazy.” Grande’s appearance on The Tonight Show marked her return to the public eye after stepping back from the spotlight once her Eternal Sunshine Tour wrapped in September. The Hollywood Reporter learned in August that the singer would be “taking a step back from visibility” for a “much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny.” Grande has faced a wave of online commentary surrounding her health and body over the last year. title: ‘Being Heumann’ Composer Francesco Le Metre Tapped Into Judy Heumann’s Drive And A ’70s Punk Rock Spirit – Sound & Screen Film
full_text: Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt ‘Being Heumann’ Composer Francesco Le Metre Tapped Into Judy Heumann’s Drive And A ’70s Punk Rock Spirit – Sound & Screen Film Alaskan Crime Procedural ‘Wild Life’ From Juliet Lashinsky-Revene In Development At NBC Untitled Signs Nnamdi Asomugha & His iAm21 Entertainment Banner View All November 9, 2026 4:45pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source For composer Francesco Le Metre , the brief when first discussing Apple Original Films ‘ disability rights drama Being Heumann with director Siân Heder was to capture the spirit of its subject, activist Judy Heumann, through music. With his score, he says, he was aiming for something “honest and intimate” — not “too big or too cinematic” — that reflected Heumann’s “personality, her drive, her humanity, but also at the same time, the impact that she had on the community.” Related Stories News Siân Heder & The ‘Being Heumann’ Crew On Creating An Inclusive Film & Production Environment – Contenders London Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Tonys, Guilds & More One throughline to the score was the sense of a “call to action” — the “big punk rock,” DIY spirit of the ’70s, which Le Metre captured through drums. “We had to deconstruct the drumming a little bit, so we played very unconventional grooves, and then also the strings,” he explained in conversation at Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film. “We performed the strings with a guitar pick instead of col legno to convey the sense of punk rock and, again, the DIY spirit of the movement.” Strings also helped, Le Metre said, to capture the sense of Heumann as someone with drive and racing thoughts who was moved to act fast. “I worked on a lot of string textures, kind of like these short phrases that were bouncing one to another. And I did the same thing with the melodic writing. When it came to her humanity as well, instead of writing a straight melodic line, I had small motifs interweaving into one another, to represent her thoughts or impulse.” Gaelynn Lea and Francesco Le Metre at Sound & Screen Film JC Olivera for Deadline Being Heumann marks the Sicilian composer’s first collaboration with Heder, the director behind another inclusive disability-themed crowd-pleaser in Apple’s groundbreaking Oscar winner CODA . Ruth Madeley stars as Heumann, who in 1977, led disabled activists in an occupation of San Francisco federal offices, refusing to leave until the government implemented landmark disability-rights protections. Others in the cast include Mark Ruffalo, Dylan O’Brien, Madeline Delp, Rob Delaney, Ray Fisher, Michael Patrick Thornton and Daniel Durant. Heder directed and co-wrote with Rebekah Taussig, adapting Heumann’s memoir. Producers include Heder, Kevin J. Walsh, David Permut, John W. Beach and Kevin Cleary. The film premiered at TIFF in September before being released in select theaters and on Apple TV this month. Watch the conversation with Le Mitre in the video above. title: 40th Australian International Documentary Conference Announces First Group Of Speakers: Poh Si Teng, Tamara Kotevska, Basil Tsiokos & More
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew 40th Australian International Documentary Conference Announces First Group Of Speakers: Poh Si Teng, Tamara Kotevska, Basil Tsiokos & More XTR Joins Oscar Contender ‘Y Vân: The Lost Sounds of Saigon,’ Award-Winning Documentary About “The Quincy Jones of Saigon” WETA And DC/DOX Partner On New $250,000 Fund To Support Documentary Filmmaking In DC Area View All November 9, 2026 4:43pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source AIDC The Australian International Documentary Conference ( AIDC ) will be welcoming some of the top talents in the documentary field to its upcoming 40 th edition. Among the first speakers to be announced: Poh Si Teng , director of Oscar contender American Doctor and founder of Tiny Boxer Films; Oscar-nominated filmmaker Tamara Kotevska ( The Tale of Silyan , Honeyland ); Basil Tsiokos , senior programmer, Sundance Film Festival; Rachel Antell, co-founder of the Archival Producers Alliance; Mandy Chang, CEO of Documentary Film Council, and Darren Dale, managing director and producer, Blackfella Films. Related Stories Podcast Doc Talk Podcast Goes Live With Director Poh Si Teng And Physicians Of 'American Doctor' Documentary 'American Doctor' Unveils Trailer, Sets Theatrical Release Date; Award-Winning Film Follows U.S. Physicians Who Treated Children Badly Wounded In Gaza AIDC, which describes itself as “the Southern Hemisphere’s premier industry event for documentary and factual storytelling,” will unfold from March 8-11 in Sydney – the first time the conference has been held in the capital of New South Wales in more than 30 years. An online marketplace follows, running from March 23-24. Watch on Deadline AIDC speakers. Clockwise from top left: Darren Dale, Poh Si Teng, Basil Tsiokos, Mandy Chang, Tamara Kotevska, and Rachel Antell. AIDC The conference also announced its theme for 2027: Reframed, which AIDC says “invites us to look at the same realities through different lenses: to ask who gets to frame the truth, and what happens when we challenge the narratives through which accepted points of view have been historically understood. “Through guest speakers and sessions, Reframed will call into question selective reframing through propaganda, misinformation, censorship and distorted realities, and will prompt us to harness alternate ways of seeing an existing truth through a contemporary lens by bringing in new, different and multiple viewpoints.” AIDC notes the 2027 edition of the conference offers the opportunity to “look back in order to look forward, acknowledging that our understanding of the world is never fixed and ever changing. Reframed asks us to reconsider what we think we know: to reveal what has been hidden, challenge what has been accepted, restore voices that have been silenced, and shine a light on what previous frames have left out.” In a statement, AIDC CEO and creative director Natasha Gadd said, “Celebrating our 40th anniversary as we embark on a new era, AIDC 2027 will be an essential gathering place for the documentary and factual sector to showcase not only what our diverse and creative storytelling community continues to create but to also actively reframe what the future could hold through bold thinking, innovative practice and radical solutions to complex sector challenges.” Gadd continued, “Through our 2027 theme, Reframed, AIDC provides a vital forum to explore and interrogate who gets to frame the truth, the forces that shape our understanding of reality, and to consider what becomes visible when we change the frame.” AIDC’s move to Sydney has been made possible by a new Principal Partnership with the government of New South Wales through Screen NSW. “Screen NSW is proud to support the return of AIDC to NSW for its landmark 40 th anniversary edition,” commented Screen NSW executive director Kylie Munnich. “With a packed line-up of compelling speakers and sessions, AIDC is set to bring together the best minds in documentary filmmaking, commissioning and financing from around the world. “We’re excited to see Sydney become a hub for discussion and collaboration, reinforcing NSW’s position as a leading destination for the screen industry. We’re also delighted to present the FACTory International Pitching Forum, which continues to connect talented creators with decision makers and to champion bold new documentary projects.” More than 750 Australian and international delegates attended AIDC’s 2026 edition. The organization announced a group of decision makers attending for the first time in 2027 along with companies new to AIDC’s market. In addition to Basil Tsiokos of the Sundance Film Festival, 2027 participants include Howard Myers-Rifai, Head of Unscripted Originals, Foxtel/Binge (Australia); Denise Barren, Assistant Director, The Whickers (UK); Aleksandra Derewienko, Head of Sales, CAT&Docs (France); Jane Nice, Head of Development, Icon Entertainment (Australia); Cynthia Paribello, Development Coordinator, Original Content, ESPN (USA), and Caden Pearson, Commissioning Editor, NITV (Australia), with more to be confirmed. Returning commissioners and funders from high profile companies in the doc and factual space include Zoe Stinson, Acquisitions and Productions Manager, TVF International (UK); Pamela Martínez, CEO/Managing Director, Limonero Films (Spain); Bo Zhang, Head of International Department – Factual, bilibili (China); Jessie Shih, Director of Program Development, PTS | Taiwan Plus (Taiwan); Choy Lin Mok, Commissioning Editor, TRT World (Turkiye); Kazz Basma, Head of Sales & Acquisitions, Sideways Film (Spain), and Paul Wiegard, Co-Founder and CEO, Madman Entertainment (Australia). These are additional program announcements made by AIDC for its 40 th edition: AIDC MARKETPLACE & INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT AIDC’s 2027 Marketplace & Industry Development Program will once again provide an expansive range of business and development opportunities specifically for documentary and factual practitioners. Alongside sales, acquisitions, and funding decisions resulting from AIDC marketplace activity, in the past seven years, AIDC’s industry development initiatives have unlocked over $3.6 million in professional and project development opportunities, and awards and prizes. Confirmed AIDC Marketplace attendees include representatives from high-profile broadcasters, streamers, distributors, sales agents and funding bodies like: ABC (Australia), BBC Storyville (UK), bilibili (China), Boardwalk Pictures (USA/Australia), Cargo Film & Releasing (USA), CAT&Docs (France), DMZ Docs (South Korea), DocPlay (Australia), Documentary Australia (Australia), ESPN (USA), Foxtel/Binge (Australia), Icon Entertainment (Australia), In-Docs | Docs By The Sea (Indonesia), Jambika Docs (Spain), Limonero Films (Spain), Madman Entertainment (Australia), NITV (Australia), Paramount ANZ (Australia), PTS | Taiwan Plus (Taiwan), SBS (Australia), Shark Island Foundation (Australia), Sideways Film (Spain), Sundance Film Festival (USA), The Post Lounge Group (Australia), TRT World (Türkiye), TVF International (UK), The Whickers (UK). The 12th edition of AIDC’s market centerpiece, The FACTory International Pitching Forum , presented by Screen NSW, is currentlyaccepting submissions, with projects sought across three strands; theCentral Showcase (for projects in development with internationalpotential); New Talent Showcase (for projects by filmmakers presentingtheir first major work); and Rough Cut Showcase (for projects seekingsales, distribution, and exhibition opportunities). Selected projects willpitch live to decision makers during AIDC 2027, and also compete for seveninternational pitch prizes from festivals and markets, including SheffieldDocFest (UK), Visions du Réel (Switzerland), Doc Edge (New Zealand),Docs by the Sea (Indonesia), DMZ Docs (South Korea), Tokyo Docs(Japan) and Hot Docs (Canada). The final submission deadline is Sunday, 8November. Meetings between industry guests and accredited producers will again take place through Cut to the Chase , AIDC’s curated meetings program for Business Pass and All Access Pass-holders. Now open for submissions, Cut to the Chase matches producers and their projects to the most relevant commissioning editors, acquisitions executives, distributors, sales agents, financiers and funders, with meetings with local and international decision makers participating in person taking place during AIDC and additional international meetings arranged online. Returning for its fourth year is AIDC’s slate-pitching program The Showroom , designed specifically for established Australian production companies with multiple non-fiction projects in development. The Showroom generates business opportunities through extended meetings and exclusive access to high-level buyers representing international broadcasters, streamers and sales agents attending AIDC. Applications open 18 November. The AIDC 2027 Marketplace & Industry Development program will also host a number of partnered initiatives, including the fifth year of the $100,000 Shark Island Foundation Feature Docs Pitch , offering up to four projects a $25,000 development grant and the opportunity to participate in the Shark Island Kangaroo Valley Development Lab; The Post Lounge Group Doc Pitch, with selected projects sharing in up to $35,000 of equity investment through development, production, and post-production support; and the $20,000 DocPlay Indie Booster, providing two independent feature documentaries at any stage, from development to completion, with up to $10,000 per project to boost their theatrical screening campaigns. Pitch meetings for each initiative take place as part of Cut to the Chase. AIDC’s philanthropically-funded program for emerging and diverse storytellers – Leading Lights – will also return for its 10th anniversary edition, featuring a tailored professional development program and the exclusive Leading Lights Pitch co-presented by AFTRS. Applications for Leading Lights are accepted until 6 December, with successful recipients receiving a complimentary AIDC 2027 Sessions Pass. 2027 AIDC AWARDS Set to close AIDC 2027 on Thursday 11 March 2027, entries are currently sought for the prestigious 7th annual AIDC Awards, recognizing outstanding completed works of new Australian documentary and factual content across a refreshed seven categories: Best Feature Documentary, Best Documentary Series, Best Factual Series, Best Documentary/Factual Single, Best Short Documentary, Best Audio Documentary and Best Digital First Documentary. Submissions close Sunday 22 November, with late submissions accepted until Wednesday 25 November (late fee applies). AIDC members will also soon be able to nominate Australian industry professionals for the fourth annual AIDC Southern Light Award, a $5,000 cash prize given by AIDC to an Australian documentary and factual industry luminary for their outstanding contribution to the sector. Opening date to be announced soon. Between AIDC’s combined Marketplace, Industry Development and Awards programs, AIDC 2027 has already unlocked access to over $275,000 in project development funding, professional development and prizes for delegates. Further announcements about AIDC’s Indigenous Creators Program and major new initiatives and pitching opportunities will follow in the coming weeks, with the full session program to be revealed 2 February 2027. title: Tina Knowles’ WACO Theater Center Sets Grand Reopening Celebration for South L.A.’s Historic Vision Theatre
full_text: × Nov 9, 2026 4:41pm PT Tina Knowles’ WACO Theater Center Sets Grand Reopening Celebration for South L.A.’s Historic Vision Theatre By Angelique Jackson Plus Icon Angelique Jackson angelique814 Latest Tina Knowles’ WACO Theater Center Sets Grand Reopening Celebration for South L.A.’s Historic Vision Theatre 4 hours ago James Bond Shocker: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult Late Contenders for 007 After Auditioning for Denis Villeneuve 3 days ago Bradley Cooper and Danny McBride’s ‘G.I. Joe’ Movie Set for 2028; Paramount Shifts New ‘Paranormal Activity’ to Halloween 2027 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source WACO Theater Center The Vision Theatre Performing Arts Center in South L.A. is reopening following 15 years of extensive renovations and a $40 million investment. To celebrate the historic theater’s return, WACO Theater Center, led by founder & artistic director Tina Knowles and executive director Shay Wafer, is hosting a grand reopening celebration in Leimert Park. “The reopening represents more than the return of a historic theater,” a release announcing the news notes. “It is a celebration of Black creativity, cultural preservation, artistic excellence and the enduring legacy of Leimert Park, a neighborhood that continues to serve as the heartbeat of Black arts and culture in Los Angeles for generations.” Related Stories Keira Knightley and 'Black Doves' Creator Joe Barton on Why Helen Should Have Been the One to Kill [SPOILER], That Oner and Hopes for Season 3 CAA's Roeg Sutherland Says It's Too Soon to Predict Fallout From Netflix Firings, Thinks Recent Mergers Represent 'Opportunity' for Industry The three-day homecoming celebration, presented by Wells Fargo, will take place Nov. 13 through Nov. 15 and feature live performances, music, entertainment and community festivities. Key events include a family-friendly, “Proud Family”-themed block party and screening of the Disney+ holiday special “A Proud Family Wizmas”; a conversation with the cast of Netflix’s “A Different World”; and an intimate evening with Club 20/20 and “House Guest with Scott Evans” sponsored by Cécred and curated by Knowles. The celebration concludes on Sunday with a live concert launching the WACO at the Vision Music Series, with a powerhouse live band led by Steve Mackey’s Taco Tuesdays, The Sessions L.A. and The Crockpock. “Leimert Park has always been a place where Black culture, creativity and community come together. To be part of bringing this beautiful theater back to life is incredibly meaningful,” Knowles said in a statement announcing the news. WACO Theater Center will serve as co-operator and co-manager of the Vision Theatre Performing Arts Center in partnership with the City of Los Angeles Department of Cultural Affairs. “The Vision Theatre represents so much history, but more importantly, it represents possibility. We want young people to walk through these doors and see a future for themselves in the arts,” Knowles continued. “We want artists to have a place where their stories are celebrated, and we want this community to know that this theater belongs to them. This is about honoring the legacy of those who came before us while creating something extraordinary for generations to come.” Originally built in 1931, the Vision Theatre stands as one of South Los Angeles’ most iconic architectural and cultural landmarks. For nearly a century, the theater’s Art Deco façade has defined the Leimert Park Village skyline. In 1990, award-winning actress Marla Gibbs purchased the historic venue, renaming it the Vision Theatre, with a dream of creating a thriving home for Black arts, culture and community. An initial renovation of the property was completed in 2011, and the current project, led by the City of Los Angeles, began in 2015. The office of Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass helped launch the partnership between WACO Theater Center and the Department of Cultural Affairs, laying the foundation for the theater’s long-term activation. Now complete, the Vision Theatre will serve as a destination for live theater, music, dance, multidisciplinary performances, arts education and community-centered cultural programming. “The renovation of the Vision Theatre unites historic preservation with state-of-the-art venue upgrades to create a world-class cultural venue that all Angelenos can be proud of,” said Daniel Tarica, general manager of the City of Los Angeles Department of Cultural Affairs. (The upgraded theater now boasts a 729-seat auditorium, a newly constructed mezzanine and balcony, expanded stage and backstage facilities and cutting-edge audio, visual and broadcast technology.) “This landmark in the heart of the creative hub of Leimert Park will be a main stage that uplifts local talent, serves as a resource for the community and will be a cultural destination for all.” Since its founding in 2016, WACO Theater Center has championed the transformative power of the arts, with a particular eye toward celebrating the rich experiences and cultural heritage of the African diaspora. Now housed at the Vision Theatre, WACO will significantly expand its reach by presenting theatrical productions, live music, dance, visual arts, multidisciplinary performances and educational programming. “The reopening of the Vision Theatre is an investment in the future of South Los Angeles and the artists who make this community extraordinary,” said Wafer, WACO Theater Center’s executive director. “Our vision is to create a thriving cultural institution that is active year-round, where artists can develop and present new work, young people can access meaningful arts education and audiences can experience world-class programming right here in Leimert Park. This is about building a sustainable home for creativity, opportunity and community connection.” All activities are free and open to the public with an RSVP. Ticketing, registration and additional program details will be available on WACO Theater Center’s website . Event sponsors include Wells Fargo, Cécred and Walt Disney Entertainment, with KBLA Talk 1580 as the media partner. title: Kris Bowers On Creating A Love Letter To Ghana & Film History With His Score For ‘The Eyes Of Ghana’ – Sound & Screen Film
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Kris Bowers On Creating A Love Letter To Ghana & Film History With His Score For ‘The Eyes Of Ghana’ – Sound & Screen Film Dominic West Joins Irish-Set Drama ‘A Weekend In The Country’ — AFM Tom Rob Smith Writing Fiction Book Based On West Memphis Three Murder Case — Thessaloniki View All November 9, 2026 4:15pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source “We wanted this score to be a love letter to Ghana and to the history of film,” Kris Bowers says of his work on The Eyes of Ghana , the latest feature from Canadian filmmaker Ben Proudfoot. The Oscar-winning musician was speaking at Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film event, where a live orchestra performed parts of Bowers’ score. Related Stories Festivals Oscar-Winning Director Ben Proudfoot Talks Historical Significance Of ‘The Eyes Of Ghana’, Scoring Doc At Abbey Road Studios & Why Project Was A “Full Circle Moment” For Barack Obama Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Tonys, Guilds & More Directed by Proudfoot, with Barack and Michelle Obama and content creator IShowSpeed on board as producers, The Eyes of Ghana spotlights Chris Hesse, the 93-year-old forgotten personal cinematographer of revolutionary African leader Kwame Nkrumah. The Eyes of Ghana details the rise and fall of Nkrumah, a towering figure of African history who served as Ghana’s first President and led decolonial efforts across the continent. Nkrumah was toppled in 1966 by a CIA-orchestrated military coup. As a result, the films made during Nkrumah’s time were ordered to be burned. Hesse is the film’s unsung cinematic hero, along with his protégé, filmmaker and producer Anita Afonu. The documentary unveils a huge archive of surviving celluloid films from Africa’s liberation era in the 20th century, which were long thought to be destroyed but were quietly safeguarded by Hesse for more than 60 years. L-R: Dela Botri and Kris Bowers perform at Sound & Screen Film JC Olivera for Deadline Bowers and Proudfoot previously worked together on the 2023 short The Last Repair Shop , which won the Documentary Short Film Oscar in 2024. The musician said he became involved with The Eyes of Ghana after Proudfoot sent him a sizzle reel of the footage he was working with. “I remember watching it in my car,” Bowers says. “After I finished watching it, I was filled with emotion just because of how much, as a Black man, my own history is lost. And it’s sad that at some point you have to give up. So, the idea that someone like Chris Hesse has preserved this history and a vision of people that look like me that I had never seen from that era made me feel incredibly moved.” The Eyes of Ghana was produced by Breakwater Studios ’ Proudfoot and Nana Adwoa Frimpong, Afonu, Bwayo and Brandon Somerhalder alongside Higher Ground’s Ethan Lewis and Vinnie Malhotra. Barack and Michelle Obama are executive producers. The film was released as a one-night theatrical event across the U.S. and Canada on October 28. It is currently enjoying a sold-out run at DocHouse in London. The film also screened at the Dikan Center in Accra, Ghana. Check out the conversation with Bowers in the video above. title: Dave Chappelle’s Charlie Kirk Joke at MSG Draws Rebuke From Erika Kirk
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All November 9, 2026 4:08pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dave Chappelle Netflix Turning Point USA CEO Erika Kirk has condemned those who laugh at political violence after Dave Chappelle made a joke referencing the killing of her husband, Charlie Kirk , during a show in New York on Saturday. Chappelle was performing for a sold-out crowd at Madison Square Garden when he delivered the bit. In it, he talked about the pressure on famous people to say and do the right things before bringing up the murder of Kirk, who was fatally shot during a speaking event at Utah Valley University in September 2025. Erika Kirk, who succeeded her husband as head of TPUSA, posted about the incident on X on Sunday. Related Stories News Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan Apologize for Laughing at "Insensitive Joke" About Charlie Kirk on 'I've Had It' Podcast News Dave Chappelle Announces Fall 2026 Arena Tour To see leftist podcasters, comedians, and commentators laugh about political assassination as though it’s entertainment and the destruction of a human life is a punchline, is beyond disgusting. My husband, Charlie Kirk, was killed in an act of political violence, something our… — Erika Kirk (@MrsErikaKirk) November 8, 2026 “My husband, Charlie Kirk, was killed in an act of political violence, something our two children and I will live with every day for the rest of our lives,” she wrote. “A culture that laughs at assassination is one of profound moral decay. It threatens the very foundation of our country and the principles that hold our democracy together. “You do not have to agree with someone’s politics to recognize the value of their life. This should not be so hard. Political violence must never be something this country tolerates, excuses, or celebrates,” she concluded. Chappelle framed the remark around free speech, pointing to the chill on public commentary that spread across media and entertainment after the shooting. “I feel fucked up saying this,” Chappelle said. “It’s scary being a public speaker. And I mean, look, ever since that guy Charlie Kirk got murdered — and I shouldn’t say this publicly — but, I feel better. I know I shouldn’t say that, but it’s just a feeling.” In the weeks after Kirk’s death, several journalists and TV personalities were suspended or fired over comments about the killing. They included then-MSNBC political analyst Matthew Dowd, who was let go after suggesting on air that the conservative activist and Second Amendment advocate had helped create the political climate that led to his assassination. The backlash culminated in ABC pulling Jimmy Kimmel Live! off the air for nearly a week over a monologue in which the host addressed the reaction to Kirk’s killing. Chappelle, who has not responded publicly to Erika Kirk’s statement, has long courted controversy with his comedy, particularly around identity politics. His material about transgender people has been a flashpoint since 2021, when his Netflix special The Closer set off internal protests at the streamer, including an employee walkout. In an interview with NPR’s Newsmakers earlier this year, the comedian said some Republicans had “weaponized” transgender jokes like his and campaigned on them. The Hollywood Reporter reached out to Chappelle’s representative for comment on the backlash and Erika Kirk’s statement but did not hear back Monday. Separately, on Saturday, Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan of the I’ve Had It podcast apologized for laughing at a joke about Kirk’s death on a prior episode. On Thursday’s episode, the hosts read posts from X about the midterms, including one that said, “We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again.” At least two of the podcast’s sponsors, Cash App and Chewy , then said on X that they were dropping their sponsorship. View this post on Instagram In an Instagram post, the hosts of the progressive podcast said laughing at the joke was wrong and announced a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety. “It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize,” they wrote. “Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence. We’ve long supported common-sense gun safety reform. To that end, we’ve made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety, the largest gun violence prevention organization in America.” On Monday, Utah District Court Judge Tony Graf scheduled Tyler Robinson, the 23-year-old man accused of assassinating Kirk, to stand trial in the summer of 2028. A statement about the delay of the trial from the Kirk family called the decision “deeply disappointing.” THR

title: David Ellison Is Very Bullish On AI’s Creative Potential
full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All November 9, 2026 3:59pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Skydance CEO David Ellison Gabe Ginsberg/Getty Images In his first earnings call as CEO at the helm of both Paramount and Warner Bros., David Ellison talked up his merged Hollywood empire as a tech-forward enterprise — and part of that tightrope walk included an embrace of AI while also dismissing “AI slop.” It’s a two-step that’s not necessarily an easy one. The technology is widely seen as a harbinger of doom for Hollywood’s traditional workflows (i.e. building sets, shooting with real background extras, going on-location, etc) while also being increasingly adapted and integrated into the business (see: Ben Affleck’s VFX firm, which has helped Netflix use AI on 300-plus titles so far, while supposedly preserving the things that make Hollywood, Hollywood). Ellison told analysts that he expects AI to help his company’s studios make content faster and cheaper, describing the technology as the biggest breakthrough in the industry since CGI effects went mainstream. Skydance plans to spend $30 billion annually across its content portfolio — that includes everything from prestige TV HBO projects to CBS procedurals and MTV reality shows as well as NFL sports rights and features at Warners and Paramount. “I don’t think it can be discounted how fast this technology is moving,” Ellison said after table-setting by saying that “in a world of AI slop we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.” Ellison has a unique lens into the issue as heir to his father Larry Ellison’s AI-powered Oracle tech fortune, which is a key facet of his effort to rebrand legacy Hollywood studios as a tech-centric venture. (To that point, the enterprise cloud apps of Oracle Fusion got a call out in the earnings call as well when talking about consolidating back office functions.) The CEO also views franchise IP — he described his empire as having 40 $1 billion franchises — as a moat protecting against the onslaught of AI content, delivering more premium experiences to his 203 million-plus subscribers at a soon-to-be merged Paramount+ and HBO Max. He then launched into an anecdote about a franchise that his Skydance Media has rebooted multiple times over the past two decades. “AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history,” Ellison bullishly said. “The last time we saw anything close to this was really the advent of CGI and digital composites in the early ’90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2 . It’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.” “If you go back in time, speaking of Terminator which everyone knows is one of my favorites, if you go back to ’83, when James Cameron made that movie it was made for $4 million,” Ellison noted. “If you wanted to make that picture today shot-for-shot, it’d be $60 million-$70 million.” The CEO added: “There’s not a lot of bets that get taken like that across our industry. And we think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budgets more digestible to take that amount of risk.” Cameron, who directed the original Arnold Schwarzenegger feature as well as its acclaimed sequel, has been one of the CEO’s biggest backers (and an early “Team Ellison” advocate as Skydance was fighting Netflix for its Warner Bros. prize). The Avatar helmer has himself been on the vanguard of the technology, with his Lightstorm banner just buying an AI-driven 3D post-production firm in September. Skydance is also looking to bake in an AI productivity narrative as it looks to find some $6 billion in cost-synergies from merging Paramount and Warner Bros. In addition to finding redundancies in corporate overhead, real estate and facilities as well as consolidating back office and corporate functions, those efficiencies include scaling AI-workflows across the combined company. That includes merging Paramount+ and HBO Max within a year, which Ellison described as an “ambitious target” that is “possible because of the latest tools in artificial intelligence.” THR

title: Skydance Bosses Throw Shade On Warner Bros Film Slate; Q4 Profit Will Take $200M Hit
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Is A Box Office Hero With $32M Live-Action Foreign-Language Opening Record, Best Ever For Gkids – Sunday AM Update ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Is King Of The Global Weekend Box Office With $63M, Towers Over ‘Ramayana’s $55M+ WW Opening View All November 9, 2026 3:53pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz Getty/Courtesy There’s a lot for Skydance co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz to be proud of in their purchase of Warner Bros . As Ellison said Monday during Skydance’s Q3 earnings call, “We have approximately $40 billion [in film] franchises which I think highly strengthen the overall portfolio,” and that “a new movie will arrive on our service every other week; film is a major driver of acquisition and engagement on our platforms.” Related Stories News Skydance Floats First Earnings Report As Hollywood Mega-Studio: Sizing Up The New Empire News Skydance Film Bosses Dana Goldberg & Josh Greenstein & The Warner Bros To-Do List: Pics That Are Ready, In The Works Or On Fire Despite potential plusses from the merger, Ellison and Kreiz also drew attention to the losses in store from Warner Bros’ 2026 film slate. More specifically, Ellison wasn’t shy in acknowledging that Paramount is in better financial waters going forward than Warner Bros on the feature side. Today’s earnings didn’t include the consolidated Warner Bros figures since the merger closed during Q4, just five weeks ago; still, Paramount brass painted a less-than-rosy picture of what’s around the corner. Watch on Deadline Said Ellison at the call’s onset, “The 2026 Paramount film slate is expected to generate $500 million more in lifetime profits than last year’s. We’ve now taken on another company with mixed results across the business…” He added, “We do have some headwinds particularly in studios where Warner Bros film has underperformed this year and will weigh on Q4 results. We’ll apply the same playbook we did at Paramount: greenlighting more selectively, prioritizing profitable streaming growth over subscriber count, optimizing linear and driving efficiency through the cost structure.” “We’ve proven it works, and we’re confident it will work again,” Ellison said, as the company is still looking at $6 billion synergies from the merger. Kreiz mentioned at the top of the call about the merger, “What I’ve seen, the various parts of the company are in strong shape. The Warner Bros. Discovery team did a good job managing their business and delivered the expected result through the close, with the one area of softness in the movie studio, and we are looking to build on their good work.” Skydance CFO Dennis Cinelli drilled down further on the red ink from Warner Bros, which saw right before the merger closed a major bomb in the Tom Cruise-starring political satire Digger , which cost $160M before global P&A and yielded $50.3M in worldwide box office. Cinelli said, “For the full year, Warner Bros is on track with our underwriting plan, with the exception of the near-term film slate. And Paramount remains on track for our 2026 guidance which is including the high-end of the profitability range at $3.9 billion adjusted EBIDTA.” The CFO added, “While the Paramount film slate continues to perform well, that will be more than offset by the continue underpeofmance of the Warner Bros film slate. Based on this, we expect to have a $200M headwind to adjusted EBIDTA in Q4. That includes films already released quarter to date as well as films that we will release going forward.” The $200M headwind is essentially Digger , more or less. There was a report out there that Warner Bros’ 2026 slate was bound to lose $800M for the full year; we know from sources that is false. Even with the expected blockbuster success of Legendary’s upcoming Dune: Part Three , the WB slate is estimated to lose around $400M, per sources. It hasn’t been a great year at the box office for Warner Bros, with global box office misfires such as Supergirl, The Bride, Digger and no film grossing more than $100M domestic. However, the Burbank lot is slightly ahead of Paramount at the domestic box office year to date, from January 1-November 9: $569M (-70% vs. same frame in 2025) to $537M (+15% vs. ’25). Combined, the two studios count $1.1 billion at the domestic box office YTD, ranking behind Universal ($1.9B), Disney ($1.6B) and Sony ($1.4B). Paramount’s high points have been Scream 7 ($121.9M domestic) and Scary Movie ($108.2M). In a further sign to Wall Street that it is cutting fat, Skydance today announced the departures of prolific filmmakers James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios’ heads . They are being replaced by early-2000s Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham, who departed the Disney-owned studio in 2017 before the explosion of Black Panther, Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame. Ellison wasn’t all poo-poo on Warner Bros today.
