full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Linda Perry Let Her ‘Let It Die Here’ Director Document “One Long Meltdown” That Resulted In A New Song, And A Movie – Sound & Screen Film ‘Tenzing’ Composer Rebekka Karijord Calls Mount Everest “Main Character” Of Movie’s Music – Sound & Screen Film Ojai Film Festival 2026 Winners — Full List View All November 9, 2026 3:30pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source In her Tribeca Festival documentary Linda Perry : Let It Die Here, Linda Perry fans were treated to a rare POV of the 4 Non Blondes frontwoman’s life and musical process. At Deadline’s Sound & Screen Film, the five-time Grammy nominee performed “What Lies with You” from her fourth solo album Let It Die Here , and recounted writing the song after going through “one long meltdown” following her mother’s death, as well as letting director Don Hardy Jr. shoot a four-hour jam session where “the song came to life in the film” after she wrote it the night before. Related Stories News Deadline Launches Its Contenders London Streaming Site Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Tonys, Guilds & More “Don and I worked on a film called Citizen Penn for Sean Penn, and then we just kind of became friends, and he asked me, ‘You know, you’re super interesting. Can I just come in your studio and film your process?’ And I was like, ‘Yeah!’ And then, I thought I would just get some good Instagram content, because I’m terrible at it. I mean, swear to f*cking god,” Perry told the Sound & Screen audience. Linda Perry sings at Sound & Screen Film JC Olivera for Deadline “And then, as it always happens when a camera shows up, things start happening,” she added. “And I was struggling a lot, I was just having such a hard time figuring out how to write a song for myself.” Perry continued, “And then Don came and said, ‘Hey, you know, the footage I’ve been shooting, I think there’s a documentary here. I’m seeing it kind of clear.’ And I was just like, ‘I don’t wanna hear about it. Don’t tell me about it. I don’t wanna f*cking know about it.’ And then, he’s like, ‘But you understand it would be about you?’ And I’m like, ‘I get it. If I said it, I said it. If I did it, i did it. But don’t bring it up to me.’ And that’s kind of how it happened.” In Linda Perry: Let It Die Here , now available to stream on Hulu and Disney+, the artist provides an intimate look at her life, career and personal struggles. title: Jessica Lange on Bringing ‘Long Day’s Journey Into Night’ Back to the Big Screen, Returning to ‘American Horror Story’ and Retirement Rumors
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All November 9, 2026 2:31pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jessica Lange ANGELA WEISS/AFP/Getty Images “You age out of a lot of parts, that’s just the nature of things,” Jessica Lange , the legendary stage and screen actress, said during a recent recording of The Hollywood Reporter ’s Awards Chatter podcast at the Virginia Film Festival , where she was being honored with the fest’s Visionary Award . The 77-year-old, who also brought to the fest her latest film, a big-screen adaptation of Long Day’s Journey Into Night , was discussing the possibility of retirement and continued, “I wouldn’t mind ending on Mary Tyrone [the protagonist of Long Day’s Journey , a morphine addict in 1912 Connecticut], let me tell you. I would embrace that, because there’s no greater part I’m ever going to play.” Related Stories TV 'American Horror Story' Finale: Paul Anthony Kelly on the Season 13 Ending: "I Was Flabbergasted" TV 'American Horror Story' Lead Joey Pollari on That Wild Jessica Lange Reveal and Up-in-the-Air Fates Headed Into Finale One of only 24 people ever and one of only 10 people still living who have won the “triple crown of acting,” as in, at least one Oscar, Emmy and Tony (she has won two, three and one, respectively), Lange has been a screen actress for 50 years. She made her film debut after being “discovered,” while working part-time as a model, and cast by producer Dino De Laurentiis in his large-scale remake of King Kong (1976). She received a huge publicity build-up, even appearing on the cover of TIME magazine. But the film proved to be such a giant flop that, she explains during this conversation, it shattered her self-confidence and almost destroyed her career. Jessica Lange in King Kong Photofest Slowly but surely, though, she rose from the ashes, first with a supporting turn in Bob Fosse’s All That Jazz (1979), then with unforgettable lead performances in films such as Bob Rafelson’s The Postman Always Rings Twice (1981), Graeme Clifford’s Frances and Sydney Pollack’s Tootsie (both 1982, and both of which brought her Oscar nominations, the latter resulting in her first win), Richard Pearce’s Country (1984), Karel Reisz’s Sweet Dreams (1985), Bruce Beresford’s Crimes of the Heart (1986), Costa-Gavras’s Music Box (1989), Martin Scorsese’s Cape Fear (1991) and Tony Richardson’s Blue Sky (1994, for which she won her second Oscar). Jessica Lange in Frances Photofest Then, as she became a mother and entered her forties, a mid-career malaise set in. For a number of years, she worked far less frequently, more often in supporting roles, and rarely in projects that excited her. That changed with the HBO limited series Grey Gardens (2009), for which she won an Emmy, and a result of her association with producer Ryan Murphy , which began soon after and encompassed four seasons of the anthology series American Horror Story (2011-2015), two of which brought her Emmys, and a single season of the limited series Feud: Bette and Joan (2017). Jessica Lange, with Drew Barrymore, in Grey Gardens Photofest But no part has enchanted her more than Tyrone in Long Day’s Journey Into Night , which she first played on the London stage in 2000 (becoming the first American actress to receive an Olivier Award nomination) and then reprised on Broadway in 2016 (winning a Tony). She spent much of the past decade trying to bring it to the big screen — a previous film version, starring Katharine Hepburn, was released in 1962 — and encountered almost as much drama as is featured in the play itself. Financing came together and fell apart numerous times, including even after the cast and crew were on set in Ireland. But ultimately, she got it across the finish line in collaboration with writer David Lindsay-Abaire and director Jonathan Kent, and she is immensely proud of the finished product. Now, as Long Day’s Journey Into Night plays at film festivals and in select theaters courtesy of a tiny distributor, Lange is hustling to make sure people know about it and see it. And having also recently returned to American Horror Story for its 13th season, which rolled out between Sept. 24 and Oct. 29, she finds herself back in contention for both an Oscar and an Emmy. For now, at least, Jessica Lange isn’t going anywhere. Jessica Lange, with Ed Harris, in the new film adaptation of Long Day’s Journey Into Night Courtesy Virginia Film Festival THR

title: Skydance Details Cost Savings and Plans HBO Max-Paramount+ Bundle in First Post-Deal Earnings Report
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All November 9, 2026 1:17pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Skydance's Ynon Kreiz and David Ellison at a press event on Oct. 6. Nate Jensen courtesy of Skydance Skydance , in its first earnings report after completing its megadeal for Warner Bros. Discovery, outlined where it expects to drive synergies and cost savings and teased a bundle of HBO Max and Paramount + for early 2027, as well as an investor day in the first half of next year. The company reported Q3 earnings Monday afternoon, with revenue of $7 billion, net earnings of $73 million and adjusted EBITDA of $1 billion, all skewed a bit by the fact that the WBD deal did not close until after the quarter ended. As a result, none of WBD’s results are included in the report, which was authored by CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz. Instead, it is the deal and what it means for Skydance’s future that will dominate the earnings conversation, with the looming bundle surely top of mind for investors and consumers, ahead of an inevitable merger of the services in the future. The move is similar to Disney’s approach with Hulu, where those two services remain distinct, but also have become increasingly intertwined. As for where the cost savings will be found? Skydance says it expects at least $2.2 billion from corporate overhead, real estate and facilities as they rationalize office space and eliminate duplicitous corporate roles; $1 billion from marketing by streamlining spend and utilizing their own platforms for more promotional work; $1.2 billion from technology as they unify tech stacks and products; $1.4 billion from procurement and vendor management. The company also says that it sees an opportunity for savings in content, though it reiterated that it still expects to spend $30 billion on content each year. “With the reach of our combined platforms across streaming, broadcast and cable, each title can work harder for us, and as one company we can make smarter choices about how we distribute and monetize our slate,” the executives wrote. title: CAA Wants to Create an AI-Generated Celebrity Advertising Machine
full_text: × Skip to main content By Winston Cho Plus Icon Winston Cho View All November 9, 2026 1:10pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source CAA chief Bryan Lourd Taylor Hill/FilmMagic Celebrity ads are getting an AI makeover. Powerhouse ad agency Ogilvy announced on Monday that it’s partnering with CAA to launch ECHO, an AI platform that allows marketers to whip up AI-generated ads featuring celebrities. The collaboration opens the door for talent to take on more endorsement deals without having to spend much more time shooting commercials while safeguarding how their digital replicas are used. The platform utilizes what CAA calls its “vault,” a database that captures, stores and licenses the digital likeness, voice and intellectual property of clients who opt in. With ECHO, brands will be able to create a portfolio of media-ready assets off of a short shoot, potentially reducing costs by as much as 75 percent and vastly reducing turnaround time, the companies said. Talent must sign off on every ad, with automated compliance engines checking AI-generated materials against contracts and brand safety guidelines. The major talent agency did not disclose which A-listers opted in to the effort. “We built The CAA Vault to ensure that talent owns, controls, and can safely monetize their digital likeness on their own terms and only with their consent,” said CAA head of strategic development Alex Shannon. “By connecting The CAA Vault to Ogilvy’s ECHO platform, CAA is giving many of the world’s leading brands a secure, consent-first activation layer, delivering full visibility and protection for talent and high-craft, verified creative at the speed of culture for brands.” ECHO’s workflow can be integrated directly into standard post-production tools. A traditional asset shoot of eight to 10 assets can be expanded into roughly 30 to 50 for the creation of ads taking advantage of buzzy TikTok trends, CAA and Oglivy said. All consumer-facing products will carry a visible watermark that reads, “[Talent Name] Approved | Recreated with AI”. In a statement, Ogilvy CEO Laurent Ezekiel said the tool solves the “fundamental tension between speed, scale and trust” in the AI era. “We are giving our clients unprecedented competitive advantage – allowing them to lead culture in real time with total trust and uncompromised craft.” The tools represents the interest in monetizing the commercial use of celebrities’ digital likenesses and, perhaps, changing views among consumers regarding the deployment of AI. Brands have largely been hesitant to wade into those waters due to pushback against deepfakes and unauthorized AI use but acceptance appears to be growing. Last month, the likeness of 1930s movie star Greta Garbo was revived in an ad from Swedish ball-bearings market SKF. ECHO is among the first to build an infrastructure around celebrities who opt into the usage of their digital replicas in ads. “We are witnessing the ‘NIL moment’ between advertising and entertainment,” said Ogilvy chief innovation officer Carol Reed. “Instead of fearing AI or using it to produce cheap volume, building ECHO in partnership with CAA proves that technology can protect artists while setting storytellers free. Our global research confirms that consumers don’t want AI to sideline the artist; they want explicit proof that the talent is in control.” THR

full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Here There Are Blueberries’ Broadway Review: Evil As Banal As A Bowl Of Fruit ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Historical Musical Plays With Gospel Truth Richard Lloyd Dies: Guitarist With Influential Punk Pioneers Television Was 75 View All June 16, 2026 5:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Paddington the Musical' Johan Persson Paddington The Musical , the seven-time Olivier Award-winning West End musical, is heading to Broadway : Previews begin Tuesday, March 30, 2027, at the Al Hirschfeld Theatre, with an official opening on Sunday, April 18. Based on the classic children’s book A Bear Called Paddington by Michael Bond and the award-winning film Paddington , the musical, by special arrangement with Studiocanal, features music and lyrics by Tom Fletcher, a book by Jessica Swale and direction by Luke Sheppard. Related Stories News Billy Crystal Sets Opening Date, Venue For Broadway Solo Show ‘860’ News Rosie O’Donnell Brings Solo Show ‘Common Knowledge’ To NYC This Summer The Broadway engagement was announced today by producers Sonia Friedman Productions, Studiocanal and Eliza Lumley Productions on behalf of Universal Music UK. Composer Tom Fletcher said in a statement, “It has been the greatest adventure of my career to be entrusted with bringing Paddington’s story to life on stage alongside my brilliant creative collaborators Jessica, Luke and our producers Sonia and Eliza. The response from West End audiences of all ages has been unlike anything I’ve ever experienced. It’s a great privilege to welcome New York audiences into Paddington’s world of curiosity and I am absolutely thrilled at the opportunity for this very rare and special bear to be on Broadway.” Watch on Deadline Casting for the Broadway production was not announced. “I couldn’t be more excited to bring Paddington to New York,” said book writer Swale. “As a city that breathes theatre, storytelling and imagination, Broadway is the perfect place to celebrate this exuberant and heart-filled story. I can’t wait. Let’s just hope Paddington loves Big Apples as much as he loves oranges.” Director Sheppard said, “ Paddington approaches life with curiosity, kindness and an unwavering sense of adventure, and what an adventure Broadway will be. It’s a dream come true to be bringing this joyful show to New York and I can’t wait for audiences to meet this very special bear that we all hold so close to our hearts.” Producers Friedman and Lumley said, “Producing Paddington The Musical with our extraordinary writing and creative team has been an immense privilege. Paddington Bear has endured for generations because he reminds us of the best of ourselves: kindness, curiosity, empathy and the belief that everyone deserves to belong. Wrapped inside a joyful theatrical adventure, with Tom Fletcher’s exceptional score at its heart, is a story about finding home, family and community in unexpected places. We have been genuinely blown away by the response to the production so far and are thrilled to be bringing it to Broadway. As the home of so many of the world’s great musicals, there is no more exciting place to produce new work than New York, and we cannot wait to share Paddington’s world with Broadway audiences.” The musical features musical supervision, orchestrations and arrangements by Matt Brind; choreography by Ellen Kane; scenic design by Tom Pye; costume design by Gabriella Slade; Paddington and puppet design by Tahra Zafar; lighting design by Neil Austin; sound design by Gareth Owen; video design and animation by Ash J Woodward; and hair, wig and makeup design by Campbell Young Associates. The West End production of Paddington won seven 2026 Olivier Awards, tying the record for the most the number of wins for any musical in Olivier Award history. The wins included Best New Musical, Best Director, Best Set Design, and Best Costume Design. James Hameed and Arti Shah shared the Best Actor in a Musical award; Best Actress in a Supporting Role in a Musical went to Victoria Hamilton-Barritt; and Best Actor in a Supporting Role in a Musical went to Tom Edden. The musical’s synopsis: “A small, lost bear from Peru arrives in London in search of a place to call home. A chance encounter with the Browns leads him into an unexpected world of adventure, where kindness has the power to change lives and strangers can become family. But London isn’t all afternoon tea and friendly faces – and even the seemingly happiest of families can have cracks beneath the surface. So, when a mysterious and vengeful villain sets her sights on Paddington, the Browns embark on a thrilling rescue mission, realizing they need this special bear as much as he needs them.” Bond’s A Bear Called Paddington was published in 1958, the first of 29 Paddington books he wrote, with the final one Paddington at St. Paul’s published posthumously in 2018. The books have sold over 35 million copies worldwide. Paddington has been adapted for television several times , first by the BBC in 1976 and most recently by Studiocanal, which developed and produced three series of The Adventures of Paddington with Heyday Films, Simon Quinn and Karen Davidson. Paddington has also been adapted as three big-screen outings developed and produced by Studiocanal with Heyday films and distributed by Studiocanal worldwide. A fourth feature film is in development with Armando Iannucci attached to the write the script with his co-writer Simon Blackwell. Also in development is a new animated Paddington feature film.
